Earth is positioned at the centre of the diagram, and the curve represents the direction and distance of Venus as a function of time.

Earth and Venus have a near [orbital resonance](/wiki/Orbital_resonance "Orbital resonance") of 13:8 (Earth orbits eight times for every 13 orbits of Venus).[[161]](#cite_note-163)
Therefore, they approach each other and reach [inferior conjunction](/wiki/Inferior_conjunction "Inferior conjunction") in [synodic periods](/wiki/Synodic_period "Synodic period") of 584 days, on average.[[6]](#cite_note-fact-6) The path that Venus makes in relation to Earth viewed geocentrically draws a [pentagram](/wiki/Pentagram#Pentagram_of_Venus "Pentagram") over five synodic periods, shifting every period by 144°. This pentagram of Venus is sometimes referred to as the petals of Venus due to the path's visual similarity to a flower.[[162]](#cite_note-Ottewel_2022-164)

When Venus lies between Earth and the Sun in [inferior](/wiki/Conjunction_(astronomy)#Superior_and_inferior "Conjunction (astronomy)") conjunction, it makes the closest approach to Earth of any planet, at an average distance of 41 million km (25 million mi).[[6]](#cite_note-fact-6)[[163]](#cite_note-MoreOrLess-165)
Because of the [decreasing eccentricity of Earth's orbit](/wiki/Milankovitch_cycles#Orbital_eccentricity "Milankovitch cycles"), the minimum distances will become greater over tens of thousands of years. From the year 1 to 5383, there are 526 approaches less than 40 million km (25 million mi); then, there are none for about 60,158 years.[[164]](#cite_note-Solex11-166)

The Ranger 1 and 2 Block I missions were virtually identical.[[46]](#cite_note-nasa-ranger1-46)[[47]](#cite_note-nasa-ranger2-47) Spacecraft experiments included a [Lyman-alpha](/wiki/H-alpha "H-alpha") telescope, a [rubidium-vapor](/wiki/Rubidium "Rubidium") [magnetometer](/wiki/Magnetometer "Magnetometer"), electrostatic analyzers, medium-energy-range [particle detectors](/wiki/Particle_detector "Particle detector"), two triple coincidence telescopes, a cosmic-ray integrating [ionization chamber](/wiki/Ionization_chamber "Ionization chamber"), [cosmic dust](/wiki/Cosmic_dust "Cosmic dust") detectors, and [scintillation counters](/wiki/Scintillation_counter "Scintillation counter"). The goal was to place these Block I spacecraft in a very high Earth orbit with an apogee of 110,000 kilometres (68,000 mi) and a [perigee](/wiki/Perigee "Perigee") of 60,000 kilometres (37,000 mi).[[46]](#cite_note-nasa-ranger1-46)

From that vantage point, scientists could make direct measurements of the [magnetosphere](/wiki/Magnetosphere "Magnetosphere") over a period of many months while engineers perfected new methods to routinely track and communicate with spacecraft over such large distances. Such practice was deemed vital to be assured of capturing high-bandwidth television transmissions from the Moon during a one-shot fifteen-minute time window in subsequent Block II and Block III lunar descents. Both Block I missions suffered failures of the new Agena upper stage and never left low Earth [parking orbit](/wiki/Parking_orbit "Parking orbit") after launch; both burned up upon reentry after only a few days.

The first attempts to perform a Moon landing took place in 1962 during the Rangers 3, 4 and 5 missions flown by the United States.[[19]](#cite_note-nasa-ranger3-19)[[27]](#cite_note-nasa-ranger4-27)[[29]](

An example of the [coastline paradox](/wiki/Coastline_paradox "Coastline paradox"). If measured using an interval of 125 mi (200 km), the coast of Great Britain has a length of about 1,500 mi (2,400 km). Using an interval of 30 mi (50 km), the length is about 2,100 mi (3,400 km).

The [coastline paradox](/wiki/Coastline_paradox "Coastline paradox") states that a coastline does not have a well-defined length. Measurements of the [length of a coastline](/wiki/How_Long_Is_the_Coast_of_Britain%3F_Statistical_Self-Similarity_and_Fractional_Dimension "How Long Is the Coast of Britain? Statistical Self-Similarity and Fractional Dimension") behave like a [fractal](/wiki/Fractal "Fractal"), being different at different scale intervals (distance between points on the coastline at which measurements are taken). The smaller the scale interval (meaning the more detailed the measurement), the longer the coastline will be.[[a]](#cite_note-1) This "magnifying" effect is greater for convoluted coastlines than for relatively smooth ones.
